facts.statement: Qianshanornis rapax is an extinct predatory bird that lived in China during the Middle Paleocene.
facts.quote: Qianshanornis rapax is an extinct predatory bird from the Middle Paleocene of China.

facts.statement: Qianshanornis rapax was smaller than the Eocene bird Strigogyps and possessed a hypertrophied, hyperextensible second toe with a claw similar to that of dromaeosaurid dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Q. rapax is very similar to the Eocene cariamiform Strigogyps, but it differs in being smaller, and in having a hypertrophied, hyperextensible second toe, forming a claw analogous to that of dromeosaurid dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that the bird's enlarged second toe helped it pin down captured prey.
facts.quote: This toe is thought to allowed the bird to better pin down captured prey.

facts.statement: Based on condylar processes, Qianshanornis rapax was likely capable of flight and may have been a superior flier compared to Strigogyps or modern seriemas.
facts.quote: Although very little wing-material is known, the condylar processes suggest it was capable of flight, and probably was a flier superior to either Strigogyps or modern seriemas.

facts.statement: Mayr and colleagues classified Qianshanornis in the monotypic family Qianshanornithidae because the specimen differed from other cariamiform birds, though they considered it unlikely to be a gruiform.
facts.quote: Mayr and colleagues only classified Qianshanornis within its monotypic family, Qianshanornithidae, since the type specimen showed little similarity to other cariamiform birds, though they at least considered it unlikely to be a gruiform.

facts.statement: Other researchers have questioned the relationship between Qianshanornis and cariamiform birds, considering its systematic affinities ambiguous.
facts.quote: Other researchers have also questioned its relationship with cariamiform birds and considered its systematic affinities ambiguous.

facts.statement: Qianshanornis lived from 66 to 61.66 million years ago during the Danian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Danian to Danian (66 to 61.66 million years ago)
